articles.title: THE ANOINTING
articles.author: J. N. Grace
articles.meeting: Word in meeting for ministry, Motueka

paragraphs.text: I have been thinking of the anointing. It has often been said that the intention is that the dispensation should finish in the way in which it began. It may be difficult sometimes to see that, but we have just been reminded that the level of things is going to be maintained in the overcomers, and I am sure we would all like to be among them. It must have been a wonderful time when the tabernacle was set up, a divine system in which God found His abode. Everything in that tabernacle was anointed with oil, and it was an oil of perfume, which of course looks forward to the fragrance of Christ, the tabernacle system in its full bearing really involving the whole universe. Think of that—finally it is the fragrance of Christ which will be before God throughout the whole universe. It refers to what came out in Christ as Man, the perfection of it, the life of Jesus so fragrant to God.

When instructions were given for the anointing oil to be made a large part of it referred to ingredients which speak of suffering (see Exodus 30: 23). Myrrh was the first component. It speaks, of course, of the sufferings of Christ. But it was not all sufferings; there were the sweet spices as well as the myrrh; so that we gather up in our minds the spirit of Jesus as here under the eye of God. What He suffered only served to bring out the fragrance that was there.

It is quite evident from the accounts we have in the gospels that the greater the pressure the more it served to bring out the perfection of that holy Man. When you think of Pentecost, you think of the Lord having completed His life here,
the fragrance of it going up to God; you think of His death having been effected and His blood having been shed, and the Spirit being poured out from on high.

It is very remarkable really that everything, everything in the tabernacle was anointed with oil, and then Aaron and his sons are brought forward. Aaron is anointed without blood, the distinction of Christ being thus foreshadowed. Then his sons are brought in, and we come into that. One was thinking, beloved brethren, of the need there is in the time we are in that the anointing should come into evidence. We are able to gather together, as on this occasion, for the service of God, in our enquiries together, and for the preaching of the glad tidings, and then we have to do with men. We long that what we do might be effective for God. We can do things rightly, we can do things intelligently, but are they effective in the divine system, bringing about something for God? Paul says, “Now he that ... has anointed us, is God”, 2 Corinthians 1: 21. What He looks for is the expression of Christ, particularly in the spirits of the saints, in the time we are in; that is why I referred to Paul and Silas in the prison in Philippi.

It is an extraordinary thing, is it not? There they were at the beginning of the extension of the glad tidings and the truth of the assembly into Europe, in the prison, suffering, their backs smitten, their feet in the stocks, and yet they were “praising God with singing”, showing manifestly the Spirit of Christ. And we may say that in one way, at the end of the dispensation, we are in a position of captivity publicly, limited maybe in our movements, and maybe things being done to the saints that have never been done in our lifetime before. What is it that God is looking to see? He is looking to see the Spirit of Christ coming out in us. Our committal is that the service of God should go on in the undiminished power of the Spirit, our hearts and souls buoyant in the sense of the One who has gone before us. He has trodden a path that we will never have to tread, and yet in the closing days of the Lord’s life here it says, “And having sung a hymn, they went out to the mount of Olives”, Mark 14: 26. I have often thought of that, coming as it does in that ‘pressure’ gospel. The Lord was equal to it all so that the spirits of His own should be buoyed up and not depressed.

So in Acts 16 it says, “the prisoners listened”. I think we little realize that the eyes of others are upon us, and the ears of others are open to what we are saying. Do they hear recrimination? Do they hear any bitterness as to what has come in by way of suffering? Who is standing for the Lord now in the midst of suffering? I think the main thing is that when the Lord looks down He sees the anointing oil coming into expression in the Spirit of Christ in the hearts and lives of His people. I think that is what brings in the answer, the divine answer; that is what brings the earthquake; that is what makes the foundations of the prison shake.

The bonds of the prisoners were loosed. That is what we want; we want to see the bonds of the prisoners loosed. And I think if we can be in keeping as to fewness of numbers—there were only two, were there not, in that gaol—if we can be in keeping at the end of the dispensation, then what God may do! He could work with the gaoler, could He not? It is the same God, the same Spirit, working, the same Spirit of Christ, the same Spirit of Jesus as where we have read.
The Holy Spirit, it says, forbade them to speak in Asia but led them to turn toward Europe.

Who could have foreseen the sufferings that were involved in the extension of the testimony as it came into Europe and its outgoings? In Australia and New Zealand it is the outgoings of Europe. It says that the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them to
go to Bithynia, but there was an area in which the Spirit of Jesus should find an expression.

Paul speaks of this in writing to the Philippians. He says, “the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ”, Philippians 1: 19. The supply lines, dear brethren, are still open, involving all that is needed for the maintenance of the testimony in conditions of suffering and pressure, so that the suffering that we are going through may be sustained in meekness of spirit.

In that anointing oil there were sweet spices, and I think they allude to the fact that it brings out something unique in the hearts of the saints of the sweetness of Christ in the midst of an area of things that as to the flesh could only bring out bitterness and hatred. Now what a triumph that is for God! That is the gospel; the same blessed gospel that was preached by Paul in that prison is available today to maintain us in the face of conflict, in the face of pressure, in the face of suffering, not only to go through, but to go through in victory, so that our brethren can be loosed from their bonds. God can act, and maybe He will. If He sees a reflection of Christ as He is looking for it and an expression of the assembly in the various localities that are available today, maybe God will come in in an unexpected way to answer the prayers of the beloved brethren.

articles.title: “THE LOVE OF THE TRUTH”
articles.author: B. M. Deck
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Motueka, N.Z.

paragraphs.text: I desire to say a little as to these two references to the truth, “the love of the truth” and then

“belief of the truth”. The first reference is over against the working of error and it seems to establish by inference that there are those who have embraced the love of the truth and are here amidst the developing conditions of lawlessness which we in our generation have to face. It is not that those who love the truth are taken out of these conditions, but they can prove salvation as morally apart, and I think the Lord would encourage us at this time to see that our position is to be faithful witnesses amidst the public dishonour that has been brought upon the name of Jesus. In divine grace there is power for testimony in persons who are marked by the love of the truth and are saved. The gravity of the times we are in should quicken a zeal for these things and appeal to the lovers of Jesus, to those who love the light and the truth of the assembly and the glad tidings.

The Thessalonians were a company of christians brought through suffering, pressure and tribulation, and they came through with spiritual spoil. This epistle is addressed to “the assembly of Thessalonians”—that is, the personnel—“in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”. It is not exactly the more formal position, as in Corinthians, but the moral formation of the personnel, “in God our Father”. It is an inward, strong position, like John in Patmos,

“in Jesus”, Revelation 1: 9. There is a peculiar glory in the time we are in—the last times. We need to gather up the spoils of these deep recovery exercises and see that there is something special reserved for the end that was not present in the same way at the beginning in the pristine days of the church.

There is nothing more urgent than that we fearlessly accept this responsibility and privilege and see what is needed now as conditions of apostasy and lawlessness develop in almost every sphere of this poor world. Where the light has once been so
bright there are now some who have, alas, fallen away because they have not been marked by
“the love of the truth that they might be saved”. We have often spoken of the term “the truth”.

Pilate said, “What is truth?” (John 18: 38), as if he neither understood nor cared to understand, but to the overcomer the truth means everything, it means more than life. How many have been martyred for the truth! It meant more to them than life. It is far more than the setting out of doctrine and principles, important as that is. It involves the revelation of God in a Man, as Paul says, “as the truth is in Jesus”, Ephesians 4: 21. Then we are told, “It is the Spirit that bears witness, for the Spirit is the truth”, 1 John 5: 6. So lovers of the truth are not just following a creed—far from it; they are following a living order of things, quickened by divine Persons and involving the knowledge of God in the Person of Jesus.

So it is a wonderful area of things when we begin to speak about “the love of the truth”. It should stir us inwardly and morally that we are called to the testimony of our Lord, of which we are not to be ashamed, “For God has not given us a spirit of cowardice, but of power, and of love, and of wise discretion”, 2 Timothy 1: 7. O, beloved, I wonder if we could just hear what the Spirit would say to us, that we should see that there is something of “the love of the truth” governing us. It is our bond, it is how the testimony can be preserved in its brightness and freshness and in the energy and vigour of life amidst the worsening conditions that are about to come under judgment. Let us therefore renew our vows and as overcomers be fully committed to the present truth. It involves the service of God, and it involves the glad tidings proclaimed in the quality of persons who come through the tribulation and sorrows of the public breakdown. In the ways of God it has all been envisaged, and the

present stress of things, where the love of the many has grown cold, will bring out the quality of persons who are bound together in love and protected by divine grace, as “using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit in the uniting bond of peace”, Ephesians 4: 3.
The second reference is to “belief of the truth”. This involves faith, and it involves the Spirit.

We have not seen the Lord yet. How wonderful it will be when we see Him; we shall be like Him then; we shall see His face. O, beloved, how our hearts are drawn to the coming of Jesus, when we shall hear His assembling shout. That time is in the Father’s keeping. Times and seasons are all in His hands—how safe they are! We go through the seasons. If it is autumn, winter, or springtime we will go through it. We have times of blessing and we have times of pressure. It is all measured; we shall not have one day longer than needed.

It is a great comfort that there are things we can do here as energised by the belief of the truth. The Lord said to those Jews in John 8, “The truth shall set you free”, and He added, “If therefore the Son shall set you free, ye shall be really free”. Let us have faith in the truth. All that God has in mind will go through and He will not be hindered in any thought of His. How wonderful faith is! How easily we get depressed, but the Lord would lift us in our spirits to see that there is an order of things untouched by death or fear; it is outside the sphere of failure. Faith and the Spirit link us with a living Man at the right hand of God. Let there be nothing else controlling us. May the Lord bless us so that we come through to His thoughts in perfection. We began the week with the thought of ‘divine perfection in a Man’ (Hymn 20), and the Spirit is here serving to bring about an answer in persons who are in the belief of the truth.

We see this when Paul says, “God has chosen you from the beginning to salvation in sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth”. It is remarkable that God has chosen us from the beginning. Think of God looking right down the dispensations and the generations of faith and working sovereignly to secure an answer in persons such as ourselves who have been recovered for such a time as this. It is “to salvation in sanctification of the Spirit”; so it is more than an outward position; salvation, as we have been taught, is not only from enemies and associations, but connects us to what is above where the final condition will be that our bodies will be changed. The position of separation and salvation here from enemies and from associations is to be in the sanctification of the Spirit, that is, an inward state that is in keeping with the position. Well, this is very searching. Some of us have been reminded recently of how valueless is separation without sanctification; more than that, it is obnoxious to God. We are called to absolute consecration. Dear brethren, this may seem a high level, but there is no other as I see it. The present moment calls for absolute committal and consecration in our love for Christ and for what is next His heart—the assembly, possessed of heavenly light which involves the revelation of God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

I would just touch Paul’s exhortation as appealing to persons who are feeling the working of lawlessness and the increase of it in violence and corruption all around us. What is to mark us? What does Paul say? “Stand firm”—let us get our feet on solid ground. “The firm foundation of God stands” (2 Timothy 2: 19)—let us get on to it, as I believe through divine grace we have. And then, “Hold fast”. It is like Revelation 3: 11, “Hold fast what thou hast, that no one take thy crown”; it is not anything public yet; it is a moral position, not an ecclesiastical one. “Stand firm”, and “Hold fast”.

As to numbers, that is in the Lord’s hand; if He wishes to add He will add ‘such as are to be saved’, but, as I see it, salvation will be in maintaining the sanctification of the Spirit. Let us not lower the standard! I believe the Spirit of God would maintain the standard inviolate. Let us be with Him and led by Him.

“Stand firm, and hold fast the instructions which ye have been taught, whether by word or by our letter. But our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and our God and Father, who has loved us”—let us remember that—“and given us eternal consolation and good hope by grace, encourage your hearts, and establish you in every good work and word”. May the love of divine Persons, known in nearness, and Their comfort, make the sense of suffering recede. What a wonderful thing it is in the days in which we are, in twos and threes, in small positions, to have a sense of divine approval—“There am I in the midst of them”, Matthew 18: 20. Well, may we be encouraged! We are in critical times, but the Lord is near.

The testimony which Caleb and Joshua rendered after their mission was that the land was a very, very good land. I think after our experience during these two days we would agree that to be in an environment which is totally different from what morally exists in the world is very good. So, as
following up what has been much in my mind this week, I want to speak of what is good. It is a great comfort in a world of evil to have a link with a God who is the Source of good.

Everything that He administers in grace to His people is good. Younger brethren, I exhort you to learn to love what is good. The Holy Spirit who indwells you will develop in you a love for what is good, not only publicly in companionships and in our walks of life, but a love for what is good for its own sake. A feature of a person who is near God is that he unvaryingly loves what is good. We are here at this time because we love what is good and hate evil. The Spirit of God has shown us that the evil in this world is on account of the rejection of Christ. So we have a judgment about it and we love what is good as it is known in the circle of God’s people. Every part of this parable of Jotham is interesting but I have chosen that part which deals with the fig because all that the fig tree says is, ‘Should I leave my sweetness, and my good fruit?’

Before I proceed with what is in mind, I would like to clarify something that was said this morning in the reading in the reference that was made to the basket of figs, because there is a deep moral lesson in it. At the time that Jeremiah wrote (see Jeremiah 24) the armies of Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonish king encompassed Jerusalem. He had come as the instrument of God’s chastisement on account of the idolatry and departure of the people and the basket of good figs represented those who bowed to the divine government and forsook the city and went into captivity. The bad figs were king Zedekiah and others who chose to remain in the city and defy the armies of Nebuchadnezzar. Now the moral lesson in that is this, that in the sight of God it is good to bow to His government. The position in Germany today is one of division of government. The world-wide scattering of the saints is governmental and any attempt

to overcome these governmental circumstances by breaking down the path of separation and opening the door to open principles is to ignore God’s government. The teaching of the Scripture is that if we humbly bow our heads in the light of what has come in, we have God’s promise that He will restore us again to the land—“For thus saith Jehovah of hosts, the God of Israel—Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be purchased in this land”, Jeremiah 32: 15. So I would say that any attempt to overcome the governmental situation by seeking the fellowship of those not walking in the path of the truth will meet God’s disapproval. Bear with me in explaining what I felt was not too clear this morning.

This fig tree says, “Should I leave my sweetness and my good fruit?”; it was fully satisfied. Brethren, are we fully satisfied? I do not mean self-satisfied, but do we find our deep satisfaction in the things of God? If Ahab had been satisfied he would not have wanted Naboth’s vineyard. The gift of the Spirit to the believer should mean that he is perfectly satisfied in what God has given him in His grace. Are you satisfied in your local meeting? Do you think you would get on better in another place? The fig tree says, ‘Should I leave my sweetness and my good fruit?’ It was satisfied. O, beloved brethren, there is great gain in developing the inheritance in our own place. So we should not leave any situation in which God is manifestly blessing us spiritually. To be blessed materially is in itself no indication of God’s favour. The thought of the fig tree is that you are satisfied spiritually. So a dignified answer is given to the suggestion that the fig tree should become king. Who wants a king’s place in this world? The King is coming—the King of kings. The Lord of lords is coming and we shall have a part in that kingdom. Who wants to be a king in his locality? Is it not far better to be among the brethren and enjoy your good fruit? Younger brethren, the service of God is greater than any service manward. I know that we sometimes measure things by platform service, but seek much grace to realize that sonship before the Father is greater than any place in service. So do not let us leave our good fruit.

In Ephesians 5: 9 it says that “the fruit of the light is in all goodness and righteousness and truth”. It is quite remarkable that goodness comes first and it is a reminder to us of the standard of walk that befits believers who have the highest light that the Lord has been pleased to give. This chapter (Ephesians 5: 11, 12) speaks of evil things and it also speaks of unfruitful things, but we should manifest the fruit of the light in all goodness. I want to speak of the great value of influence amongst the brethren. It is an expression that is often used, ‘an influence for good’. Beloved younger brethren, seek the help of the Lord that you are always an influence for good in every way in which you move in the circle of the saints. It is not that you need to exhort or preach to your companions. Influence is a very subtle thing, and I use the word subtle in a good sense. The effect of good influence permeates the saints. So the fruit of the light is goodness and involves a standard of conduct that reflects God.

So in John’s epistles “beloved” is one of his favourite designations. It is good to think of and address the brethren affectionately. So he says, “do not imitate what is evil”. The imitation of evil is more readily done than the imitation of good, and anything which detracts from the rights of Christ is not good. If there is a lowering of the standard of the truth it does not come from God who is the Source of good. We are not called upon to imitate what is evil. We must adhere to a standard. In 2 John 9–11 the question arises as to a person that comes to the house not abiding in the

doctrine of the Christ. What do you think John would say if someone were to say to him, ‘It would be good to have that man in the house?’ Would he say that was good? No, he would say, “Do not receive him”. Love is not incompatible with the maintenance of the truth. Is there a brother or a sister with a difference with another? Take the opportunity to imitate God. What did He do? He forgave us—what a line to imitate! The pattern of assembly life in the character of our meetings is a good thing. We want to imitate everything that is good in the assembly. Assembly customs, if they are not local customs, are good things and should be imitated. John says, “He that does good is of God”.

There is sometimes a charge laid that we are not very evangelical. Well, there was a little maid in Naaman the Syrian’s house and all that she did was good because she learnt through the prophet that God was good. She was evangelical. I do not accept the suggestion that the saints are not evangelical. There is abundant scope for evangelical work in personal contact, in giving out tracts, in the open-air preaching, each of which is good, there are examples that could be quoted from the New Testament, one of which is that of Andrew who first found his own brother. That is a fine place to start, first finding your own brother. What influence for good have you in the home, that you can bring your brother to Christ?

“He that does good is of God”—in a corrupt world the saints of God are like the salt of the earth. Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its savour wherewith shall it be salted? The trend of the meetings these two days is to alert us to the fact that the salt must not lose its savour. The great preservative of the gospel is the people of God themselves going on with what is good.
“He that does evil has not seen God”. How do you see God?

That is a big question. It is not with physical eye-sight. You see God morally in the death of Christ. You see the solution of good and evil on the cross and if you do evil you ignore God’s judgment at the cross. If you do good you bear testimony to the triumph of good over evil.
Remember that God is the Source of good and let our time be filled out here amongst the brethren and amongst men in the pursuit of what is good, for His name’s sake.

That this is a rather unfamiliar scripture you will readily perceive, and I want only to make an application of it. I sometimes wonder about some scriptures as to why they are in the Bible, but “Every word of God is pure”, Proverbs 30: 5. I do not know whether you read your Bible—most people here do, some read it more than others—but it is a good book to read.

Read a little every day, and because it is reading night, do not think that will do for that day. Develop the habit of reading something yourself, by yourself too perhaps. When I was first starting out to work (we had to start at half-past seven) my father used to get up and make my breakfast and insist on reading with me. I think he realized that I did not read up in my bedroom. I tumbled out of bed and all I wanted was my breakfast and then a run to the station; but he insisted on reading—and I sometimes used to bless him for it too! But “Every word of God is pure”, and God has

not left any one of us here without direction. There are all kinds of questions which come up during our lives, the answers to which are in this book. These include involved questions that persons have debates about and which the social service people have conferences about, quite simple answers to which are given in this book. I would encourage you to read your Bible.

Now this is a section that, as you will be aware, we are inclined to skip over or take two chapters together. I am not sure that we are always wise in that. Sometimes the unexplored parts of Scripture are very yielding. This chapter is speaking about a certain matter and I do not speak about the matter directly, the literal thing that is being referred to. It is not my intention to comment on that at all; I do not know that I could. But I want to make an application of the scripture and suggest that it bears the application that as a believer you may begin to find some stirring of life in you. It speaks about a woman conceiving—there is some stirring of life. Something comes into your mind, maybe in a meeting like this, which was not there before; something begins to stir in your mind and in your soul. It may just be that some ray of light from God comes into my soul, that I begin to see something in the truth that I have not seen before. It is not exactly that I hear mere information but that some light from God, some divine impression that has come from God Himself, begins to affect me.

That is intended to be a constant experience, dear friends, that light from God, some ray of the truth, comes home to me with force and with power, and something living begins to stir as a result. You could not explain it; you had perhaps heard that expression many times; it had gone over your head; but quite inexplicably something that you may have heard perhaps a dozen times suddenly takes on vitality and meaning and reality, and you realize in your soul that something has happened. It may be just that you see something in an objective way; I think that may be in the suggestion of the bearing of the male; it is not exactly that you can say that you are up to it, but you see something. The objective truth is very fine; it is presented to us as something to lay hold of; it is arresting; it is a sight; it is the idea of a sight, something that comes before your view and you are affected by it, you are stirred in relation to it.

Now the associated exercise is quite something to go through because you find in yourself that there is that which would quench it. If light from God is presented to us, Satan will always and immediately bring in a kind of counter-attraction. He did that with Abraham. The glory of God appeared to him, and he went so far on the strength of it, and then he got stuck.

Now we all know what that is, that you are moved, maybe by a powerful presentation, a preaching, you are moved in your soul, and you make a certain journey and then you get bogged down. So the exercise may be quite prolonged and includes a period of seven days and then a period of thirty-three days—a time that no doubt involved for this person a time of reflection as to what it all meant and what was involved in it and how personally one finds what is mixed, what is spoken of here as uncleanness. And yet I have light, I have precious light from God, but I find this mixed condition with me. You find, if you get any impression of Christ, Satan will certainly bring in a counter-attraction, he will certainly do that, and we find in ourselves what will respond to it.

But then there is even more than that because the scripture goes on to speak about the possibility of the bearing of a female. Now often in Scripture the female represents what is subjective. You would not get that idea from the world, would you? but that is God’s thought that what is feminine is subjective, so that “the assembly is subjected to the Christ” (Ephesians 5: 24); the feminine conveys the idea of what is subjective, what is subject and subjective.

Now we use these words but I do not know if we all understand too well what they mean. I will just tell you what I understand; I think that when Christ is presented to you objectively it is like a ray of glory which you see and which affects you, but what we speak of as the subjective side of the truth means that I embrace the process of making that my own, of actually grasping it and having it for myself. It is not that I am content to leave it there in the distance, even though I can see it clearly; if I am going to get over to the side of formation I have got to make it my own. That becomes costly; you will notice here that for that side there are fourteen days, there is double the time, and then there are sixty-six days—not thirty-three days—there is double time again, and I think every one of us here would acknowledge that the actual getting into the good of an impression is quite a prolonged exercise, it is quite extended. And do you know why that is? It is because if Christ is to be formed in me, something of me has to be displaced to make room for it. It is a cardinal principle in physics that no two portions of substance can occupy the same space at the same time, and if Christ is going to be formed in me, something of me will have to go to make room for Him, and that is quite prolonged, is it not? It is; whether you think so or not, it is; it is quite prolonged, and it is quite difficult and testing. But it is worth it.

You can see it with Rachel that the bearing of Benjamin, which really means Christ formed in the saints, was costly to her, but it was worth it because Benjamin had the key to a critical situation at a certain time later on, and things cannot be worked out fully, dear brethren, just on the objective line. The full result must involve the actual going through the exercise that Christ should be really formed. Now you love Jesus, do you not? Do you remember what He did for you? He came down of His own volition; no one made Him come down. He came down here to this world of sin and woe, and He was abused by men, but He went to the cross, and most of us can say that there He bore our sins in His body. You do not wonder that we love Him, do you? It is quite reasonable, it is the most rational thing to do to love Jesus. It is quite irrational not to love Him. But you love Him, and I tell you that in principle you can embrace Him. This woman here would actually one day embrace the son or the daughter. So that whilst the exercise may be prolonged, it is worth it. You may be going through exercise and you may be troubled—you will be too; that would be the normal thing; but the end is worth it. I would encourage you to hold on and to remember that whilst there are the days of uncleanness, there are also the days of cleansing.

Now there is a distinction there, which has been pointed out by another. There are seven days of uncleanness, but there are thirty-three days of cleansing, and there are fourteen days of uncleanness but sixty-six days of cleansing. Now it is a great thing to get past that side of uncleanness into the area of cleansing. The cleansing period is not that the exercise is complete, but it is moving that way. Dear brethren, you know, the Scriptures are wonderful, are they not?—How rich they are! I am only scratching the surface here. There would be at least seven applications to this scripture, I think, because it speaks in the Psalms that the words of Jehovah are “purified seven times”, Psalm 12: 6. I am only giving one application of it, but it is just the one that seems to be laid on me, and I would like to encourage us here, and especially you dear young ones, to go on with your exercises and reach these days of cleansing because you will find it will be worth it, and there is not one of us here who has not had sorrow and known what displacement is, and known what it is to cry at night and to be thoroughly downcast with ourselves. But you will find the Lord is always tender, and even if others do not understand you, you will find the Lord always will.

May every one of our hearts be drawn to Him so that not only do we see Him objectively in His beauty and His glory, but He is actually formed in us. How appropriable we will be! How increasingly we will feed on one another as He is formed in us, actually formed. You can go to a person and appropriate him or her as some feature of Christ is formed there. Let us press on until this is so more and more, dear brethren, for the Lord’s name’s sake.

I was reading in the past week some ministry at Valence in 1939 by Mr. Taylor (N.S. Vol. 74, p.381) in which he read from John 6, where the Lord came near to the disciples, walking on the sea to them. He spoke of the way the Lord draws near to His own. The difficulties were very great; the Lord had been on the mountain by Himself, no doubt in prayer. But it says—
“And Jesus had not come to them, and the sea was agitated by a strong wind blowing”

(John 6: 18). No doubt it was hard work rowing; the Lord knew all about this. It was dark and it was rough, and He drew near to His own. They saw Him walking on the sea and coming near the ship, and He said, “It is I; be not afraid. They were willing therefore to receive him into the ship”. That ministry has affected me, because that is our current experience. The night is dark and the rowing may be difficult; the wind is against us; but everything is known to the Lord and He draws near to us. I am sure we can say we are willing to receive Him. He constantly comes to us, saying, “It is I; be not afraid”. So one has been thinking of the Lord being with His own.

In Daniel He was with these three faithful men. The whole power of the Chaldeans was against them. Nebuchadnezzar was full of rage and fury; all his power was against these faithful men. But what a fine statement they make—“Be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image that thou hast set up”. It makes one think of Paul saying, “I make no account of my life as dear to myself”, Acts 20: 24. These men did not hold their lives dear. Their faithfulness to God was absolute. They say to the king, “We will not serve thy gods”. May this spirit be with us, that we do not serve Satan, or the world, or the law of sin, but are committed to the will of God. It seemed outwardly that God was not with these three men, because they were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace. God allowed things to go so far. It reminds us of the martyrs—how many there have been. How heaven honours them! And we honour them. What a place they will have in the kingdom! And many are in the furnace now. We have thought of some in New Zealand; there is indeed a furnace there of suffering for the truth.
But then they were not three but four in the midst of the fire—“Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt;

and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of God”. How touching this is, illustrating how the Lord Jesus goes through the sufferings with His faithful ones. This is a remarkable statement—‘Lo, I see four men loose’. They are no longer bound; the bonds had been loosed and they were walking in the midst of the fire. How pleasing this is to the Lord: all Satan’s power is against them, but they are walking in dignity, and they have the company of one “like a son of God”. We might say, in applying this scripture, that it suggests walking in the truth, working out the truth of the assembly. This applies in this place where we are today.

Then we think of our brethren, for example, in eastern Europe, with so much against them, but walking in the truth, walking in liberty and dignity, and the Lord is with them. How the Lord would delight to give them His company!
These three men were brought through in a complete way, in absolute triumph and victory

“these men, upon whose bodies the fire had had no power, nor was the hair of their head singed, , neither were their hosen changed, nor had the smell of fire passed on them” (Daniel 3: 27). It would give us a sense of victory. There is what Satan cannot touch or damage. The Lord said, “Hades’ gates shall not prevail against it”, Matthew 16: 18. May we be comforted by this, that the Lord is with us, and God is with us. Paul says, “If God be for us, who against us?”, Romans 8: 31. And speaking from experience, he says elsewhere, “At my first defence no man stood with me, but all deserted me ... But the Lord stood with me, and gave me power”, 2 Timothy 4: 16, 17. The Lord looked at that lonely man and saw everyone leave him alone. It is as if the Lord would say, ‘I will stand with him’. So Paul says, “But the Lord stood with me, and gave me power”. What an experience for Paul; all alone, but the Lord with him. That experience is available to us.

In John 14 it is the inward side, the wonderful setting out of how divine Persons are with the saints, those who keep His commandments; firstly, “another Comforter”, with us for ever, and then the Lord: says, “I am coming to you”. How He loves to come; the saints are attractive to Him. It says in chapter 20 of this gospel, “Jesus came and stood in the midst”

(John 20: 19); that company attracted Him. The disciples were there, the doors shut, and Jesus came. Thank God, we experience this, particularly at the Supper, but also in our other comings together. We experience the truth of these words, “I will not leave you orphans, I am coming to you”. How precious this is, that we can leave behind the world and the opposition and be lifted up in the company of the Lord. He goes on to say, “Yet a little and the world sees me no longer; but ye see me; because I live ye also shall live”. He presents Himself to us.

As we read the Scriptures the Spirit brings Christ before us and He gives us the experience of life in Himself, experience of the realm in which He is. “In that day ye shall know that I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you”; He is in the Father; what a place is His in the Father’s affections. But we are in Him, so that we have entrance into that home of love, where the Father’s love to Christ is known, whilst the Lord Jesus loves to speak to us of the Father. How precious these things are! The Lord says, “In that day ...”, that is this day, the time of His absence, but the time of the experience of His presence as He draws near to those He loves. We could say, speaking carefully, He cannot remain away where conditions are right.

Finally, in 1 Corinthians 14, it is God coming among us by means of His word. This section is about prophecy. This should come into every occasion, the living, present word of God, and yet not only His word, but God Himself. So here someone comes in, an unbeliever or a simple person, and what

he reports is that “God is indeed amongst you”. It is a most remarkable thing. Paul goes on to speak in detail of a particular occasion which God honours and comes into. It makes us very reverent and very careful, but how blessed it is, how comforting, how encouraging, that “God is indeed amongst you”. It is like the mercy-seat in the tabernacle. God said, “There will I meet with thee, and will speak with thee from above the mercy-seat”, Exodus 25: 22. God loves to be thus among His people, that they should know His presence and hear His living word. It is said, “When Moses went into the tent of meeting to speak with Him, then he heard the voice speaking to him from off the mercy-seat”, Numbers 7: 89. This is one of our greatest privileges, the presence of God and the word of God; “God is indeed amongst you”.
Thus God comforts and encourages His beloved people, and it is the same whether we be many or few.

We have a nail in the holy place. We have an abiding place in the holiest of all in that sense—a sure footing there, for Christ is there. The nearer you get to God, the more sensitive you become of your acceptance. I repeat that. The nearer you draw to God the more conscious you are of the delight He has in you in Christ. The further you are away, the more the enemy has the advantage, for you are not conscious in the same way of the divine love and interest in you.
